newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sanyo Sec has no loan agreement as deadline nears.
newsitem.headline: Sanyo Sec has no loan agreement as deadline nears.

text.p: Sanyo Securities Co Ltd said on Thursday it still had not reached agreement with nine life insurers on its request to delay loan repayments, with a deadline for an accord looming at the end of the day.
Worries that a last-minute agreement may not be reached helped push Sanyo Securities' share price to a record low on the Tokyo Stock Exchange on Thursday.
"No conclusion has yet been reached," a Sanyo spokesman told Reuters.
He offered no further details and said the second-tier Japanese brokerage at the moment had no plans to make public the outcome of any further talks, or lack thereof, with the insurers later today.
Officials at several of the life insurers confirmed that there was no pact yet on delaying the 20 billion yen worth of subordinated loans from insurers, which fall due at the end of July 1998.

Spokesmen for Nippon Life Insurance Co and Dai-Ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co told Reuters that Sanyo had yet to offer anything new in the face of their requests for the brokerage to work out a new restructuring plan in exchange for the delay.

If the insurers do not agree to a delay by the end of Thursday, Sanyo's capital adequacy ratio could fall below 120 percent, a level at which the Finance Ministry may order the brokerage to take more drastic restructuring measures to improve its operations, industry sources said.

Some sources said that insurers may make an 11th-hour "political decision" and agree to a delay, taking into consideration the likely negative impact on the securities industry if Sanyo is forced into a ministry-mandated restructuring.

Lingering financial jitters over Sanyo, burdened with bad assets at its financial and real estate affiliates, pushed the brokerage's shares to an all-time low of 138 yen on Thursday. As of 1 p.m. (0400 GMT), Sanyo's shares had recovered slightly to 141 yen, down three from Wednesday's close.

Subordinated loans are repayable only after debts with higher priority have been honoured. Moreover, subordinated loans cease to be regarded as part of an institution's capital once the remaining period to maturity falls below one year. At that point, the loans are treated as short-term debt.
In 1994 Sanyo embarked on a nine-year restructuring plan to help bail out its non-bank financial affiliates with the support of three major creditor banks and Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
Nippon Credit Bank Ltd (NCB) said on Wednesday that it would cooperate with the two other main banks and Nomura to support Sanyo, Jiji news agency reported.
NCB vice president Shigeoki Togo, due to take over as the bank's president next month, was quoted by Jiji as saying that it was likely that life insurers will comply with Sanyo's request for a delay.
